analysis.one_liner: Makes public colleges and tribal colleges tuition-free for students and cuts federal student loan interest rates.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by Rep. Jayapal with 21 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and died there without a markup, hearing vote, or floor vote in the 116th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a federal-state partnership to eliminate tuition and required fees for students without a bachelor's degree at community colleges, public four-year universities, and tribal colleges, with the federal government covering roughly two-thirds of the cost ($48 billion authorized for fiscal 2020) and states covering about a third. It would also have funded grants to eliminate or sharply reduce tuition for low-income students at private historically Black colleges and minority-serving institutions, expanded federal work-study and TRIO/GEAR UP programs, and let borrowers refinance federal student loans at rates as low as 1.88 percent.
analysis.who_benefits: Students without a bachelor's degree attending community colleges, public four-year universities, or tribal colleges would pay no tuition or required fees, regardless of income. Low-income students at private historically Black colleges and minority-serving institutions would see tuition eliminated or sharply reduced. Federal student loan borrowers could refinance at rates of about 1.88 percent. Low-income students receiving the maximum Pell Grant would have their remaining cost of attendance covered by institutional aid.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students at public and tribal colleges

how_it_helps.text: The bill authorizes grants so states and tribal entities can eliminate tuition and required fees for all eligible students at community colleges, public four-year institutions, and tribal colleges, with the federal share at 67 percent and a 33 percent state match.
Private nonprofit historically Black colleges and minority-serving institutions would receive $1.34 billion in fiscal 2020 to eliminate or significantly reduce tuition for low-income students.
Federal Direct Loan borrowers could elect to refinance their loan interest rate to roughly 1.88 percent at any time during the life of the loan.
States must maintain instruction spending per student and need-based aid at 2017-2018 levels, and within five years at least 75 percent of instruction must come from tenured or tenure-track faculty.
Federal Pell Grant recipients at participating institutions would receive institutional aid covering the full gap between their cost of attendance and their Pell Grant and family contribution.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the bulk of the program (about $48 billion for fiscal 2020, then open-ended sums through 2029), and state governments would bear a 33 percent match plus requirements to maintain 2017-18 levels of instruction spending and need-based aid. Lower loan interest rates would reduce federal student loan program revenue.

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates about $48 billion for fiscal 2020 and open-ended sums for fiscal 2021-2029 with no offsetting revenue in the bill, so the full cost falls on federal borrowing or future appropriations.

States must cover 33 percent of the cost and maintain 2017-18 funding levels to participate, which could strain state budgets and give states a reason to opt out, leaving their students without the benefit.
Cutting student loan interest to 1.88 percent would substantially reduce revenue from the federal Direct Loan program, though the bill would redirect any program surplus to the Pell Grant program.
The tuition waiver is not means-tested — any student without a bachelor's degree qualifies — so some benefits would flow to families who could otherwise pay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large and broad: free tuition at public colleges would eliminate a major cost barrier for working- and middle-class students, and the bill includes guardrails (state funding maintenance, tenure-track requirements, bans on using funds for stadiums or merit aid) designed to keep quality from eroding. The honest costs are real: roughly $48 billion a year in new federal spending with no dedicated funding source, a state match that some states might refuse, and loan refinancing terms that reduce federal loan revenue. The design is more disciplined than many tuition-free proposals, but its price tag is large and open-ended.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Education and Labor Committee on the same day and never received a markup, hearing vote, or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the College for All Act of 2019 on June 25, 2019, with 15 original cosponsors including Reps. Omar, Ocasio-Cortez, Khanna, and Pocan.
The bill attracted 21 cosponsors, all Democrats, over the life of the bill.

The House referred it to the Committee on Education and Labor on the day of introduction, and the action history shows no further action — no committee markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote — through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Institutions that charge tuition — including for-profit colleges and private institutions outside the bill's minority-serving carve-out — kept the status quo, and the federal treasury avoided roughly $48 billion a year in new spending. Students at public colleges kept paying tuition.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tuition-charging colleges and the federal treasury

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the College for All Act of 2019 in the House.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Committee of referral; Chairman Rep. Bobby Scott (D)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or committee vote after its referral; the bill's action history shows no activity beyond referral.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 cosponsors were Democrats and there were no Republican cosponsors; no floor or committee vote ever occurred, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: Federal grants would flow through public institutions and tribal colleges to wipe out tuition, making them the permanent channel for a free-public-college guarantee, while locking in state funding floors and tenure-track requirements that strengthen them.

The bill excludes for-profit institutions from its grant programs and bars newly nonprofit institutions with for-profit origins from eligibility for 25 years, undercutting the tuition-charging model they profit from.

industries.industry: Private nonprofit historically Black and minority-serving institutions
industries.note: They would receive $1.34 billion in fiscal 2020 to eliminate or sharply cut tuition for low-income students, subject to tuition-increase limits and aid-maintenance conditions.
They receive no funding under the bill, and a tuition-free public option would draw students away from institutions that depend on tuition revenue.

industries.industry: Federal Direct Loan program (federal loan revenue)
industries.note: Refinancing to a 1.88 percent rate would sharply cut the interest income the federal government collects from student borrowers, though any program surplus would be redirected to Pell Grants.
